summary: Connecticut's oldest standing light: a 1760 harbor light, its 1801 stone tower, the fog trumpets, and the keepers who worked it until 1912.

structures.note: First tower, 64 feet tall (NRHP and LighthouseFriends), replaced by the 1801 tower

access.note: Keeper's dwelling is privately owned. The tower is owned by the New London Maritime Society; the tower and grounds are closed except on the Society's special tours (LighthouseFriends).

The standing tower was built 1800-1801 (NRHP). The 1760 tower was replaced. Propose a separate row for the 1760 tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1760 and 1801 tower dates both belong to this station. The 1760 tower (64 feet, stone) was replaced by the present tower, begun 1800 and finished 1801 (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).
NRHP gives 1760 for the first light on the site; LighthouseFriends says the first tower was finished in 1761; USLHS gives 1789 as the year the station was established under federal control.
NRHP says a Fresnel lens came within a decade after an 1850 inspection, and that the Lepaute lens may be the original equipment. LighthouseFriends gives 1857 for a fourth-order Fresnel lens.
LighthouseFriends says a steam whistle came about 1857; NRHP records a fog-signal engine by 1869. Both may be right; the NRHP does not mention a whistle.
NRHP gives 5 May 1800 for the congressional appropriation of $15,700; LighthouseFriends gives 7 May.
The Board's 1899 report records the old fog-signal house converted into an oil house; the NRHP and the 1900 report date it to 1900.
LighthouseFriends says automated 1912. NRHP says the fog signal moved to New London Ledge in 1911. The USLHS roster's last head keeper is Woods, 1911-1912.
The National Register form says the federal government assumed responsibility for the lights by 1789; LighthouseFriends dates the cession of this light to May 1790. The story gives both.
The 1899 report already lists the old fog-signal house as converted into an oil house; the 1900 report and the National Register form date the conversion to 1900. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Roster: all 29 USLHS lines entered as printed (USLHS place page, cached). NRHP spells the 1818 contractor 'Crandall' and the 1833 OCR 'Klmball'; the story uses the roster spelling Kimball. Joseph F. Woods appears on the New London Harbor roster (head keeper 1911-1912, also first assistant 1911). The USLHS archive's person record for Joseph F. Woods (https://archives.uslhs.org/people/joseph-f-woods, source 13) lists the same man at New London Harbor, then Cold Spring Harbor (1912), then Saybrook Breakwater (1912-1918); the two Woods roster lines carry that person slug, and the story cites the person record for the Saybrook stint. LighthouseFriends does not connect the two stations in its text. The Board's proposal for a light and steam fog-signal station on the southwest ledge is headed 'Black Ledge, New London Harbor' in the 1891-1900 reports. The NRHP form says the fog signal moved in 1911 to the new New London Ledge Lighthouse. No source read says whether the two are the same site, and the story does not say so. The NRHP form names the 1980s keeper's-house occupant; that private resident is deliberately not named here. LighthouseFriends names the 1928 buyer of the keeper's dwelling, a private resident, and the story does not name her. Only LighthouseFriends sources the 1903 siren complaints, the 1841 Munn/Mason dismissals, and the 30 May 1912 rescue account; Woods's account is quoted as LighthouseFriends prints it. Chronicling America searches for 1903 siren and 1912 items returned no pages. The 2019 zoning figures are from LighthouseFriends' text and may have changed; check the Society before a visit. The USLHS place page says the site is open to the public; LighthouseFriends says the grounds are closed. The story follows LighthouseFriends and the owner-steward arrangement. The record's height (27.0 m), characteristic 'Iso W 6s' and range 17 nm are not sourced in this file and are not repeated in the story. Quotes from the Board's 1896-1900 reports come from OCR text; OCR errors are kept in the evidence quotes. The 1899 quote keeps the OCR word 'oonverted'. The 1897 report's 3-1/2 horsepower figure is OCR'd as '3J-horsepower' on scan page 313; the NRHP gives 3-1/2, so the story cites both. The 1900 date for the oil-house conversion differs from the 1899 report (see resolved_conflicts); the story states both. The 1900 keeper's-dwelling addition is cited to the report for the year ended 30 June 1900. Fact-check 2026-10-22: 'did not seem to hear the horn' hedge restored; the 'Black Ledge' proposal and the New London Ledge light are not linked; 'Pequot Avenue' views corrected to limited views; metres added to feet.
